newsitem.title: USA: Lockheed Martin sets up independent company.
newsitem.headline: Lockheed Martin sets up independent company.

text.p: Lockheed Martin said Thursday it planned to form an independent communications technology company out of 10 of its business units.
The company, L-3 Communications, will be co-owned by Lockheed, Lehman Brothers Capital Partners III LP and a management team of former Lockheed executives.
The $525 million deal is expected to close within 45 days. Lehman will own about 50 percent of, L-3 Communications; Lockheed will retain 35 percent, and the management team will have 15 percent.
In a separate announcement, Lockheed and British Aerospace said from London they planned to bid for a new U.S. and British army scout car and reconnaisance vehicle.
A spokesman for Lockheed told Reuters the deal was worth a potential $5 billion "if the U.S. and British armies order what they say they need."

British Aerospace said in the statement the two companies would form a team to develop a vehicle for TRACER/FSCS (Tactical Reconnaissance Armoured Combat Equipment Requirement/Future Scout Cavalry System).

Lockheed said the L-3 communications company would be formed by combining Advanced Recorders in Sarasota, Fla.; Communications Systems in Camden, N.J.; Conic in San Diego; Display Systems in Atlanta; Hycor in Woburn, Mass.; Microcom in Warminster, Pa.; Narda Microwave in Hauppauge, N.Y., and Rancho Cordova, Calif.; Randtron in Menlo Park, Calif.; Telemetry & Instrumentation in San Diego; and Wideband Systems in Salt Lake City.

Headquarted in New York City, L-3 will have 5,000 employees and combined 1996 revenues of more than $650 million. Its chairman and chief executive will be Frank Lanza, who was president and chief operating officer of Loral Corp. when it combined with Lockheed in 1996. Robert LaPenta will be president and chief financial officer, Lockheed said.
Lockheed stock was down $1.875 at $79.625 in midday trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
